evidence.excerpt: Standard cost-of-quality optimisation models derive an optimal inspection level by balancing appraisal and failure costs under assumptions of steady production volume. In high-mix low-volume assembly, batch sizes fluctuate widely and setup-to-run ratios are high, making these assumptions inappropriate. This paper formulates a cost model in which appraisal intensity (fraction of output subjected to each inspection stage) is chosen per batch given known batch size, product-specific baseline defect probability, and a per-unit inspection cost that includes setup amortisation. The model is solved analytically for single-stage inspection and numerically for two-stage inspection with in-circuit test followed by functional test. Using data from three product families (n = 847 batches over 18 months), the model yields appraisal intensity recommendations that differ from the company's fixed-sampling plan by −15% to +38% depending on batch size. Simulated application of the model reduces total quality cost per unit produced by an estimated 9.3% relative to the current fixed-intensity plan. Sensitivity analysis identifies defect probability estimation accuracy as the dominant uncertainty driver.
